name: Pediatric antegrade ESIN entry approach to the femur
corridor: Lateral trochanteric incision to paired anterolateral metaphyseal entry points distal to the greater-trochanteric physis

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the proximal lateral femur accessible and the entire femur imageable.

setup.text: Template nail diameter, contour, entry separation, and distance from the greater-trochanteric physis before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark greater trochanter, its physis under fluoroscopy, lesser trochanter, femoral shaft axis, and planned paired lateral entries.

incision.text: Make a 3-5 cm lateral trochanteric incision extending proximally from the planned entries to permit angled nail advancement.

superficial_interval.text: Spread fascia and lateral muscle fibers bluntly to the anterolateral femoral cortex.

deep_interval.text: Create two controlled lateral metaphyseal entries 0.5-1 cm distal to the trochanteric physis, separated at least 2 cm axially and 1 cm on the lateral plane.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, lateral muscle, periosteum, then proximal femoral metaphyseal cortex.

structures_encountered.text: Fascia lata, abductor-vastus region, greater-trochanteric physis, proximal metaphysis, and medullary canal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Greater-trochanteric physis, proximal femoral cortex, abductors, lateral femoral cutaneous branches, and femoral-neck blood supply are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Entries too close together can split the cortex; proximal or medial misplacement risks the physis or femoral neck.

retraction_hazards.text: Use blunt spreading rather than aggressive muscle stripping and protect soft tissue from rotating nail ends.

exposure.text: Provides paired antegrade elastic-nail access while avoiding the distal fracture and knee.

limitations.text: Requires adequate proximal metaphyseal space, appropriate fracture pattern, and careful growth-plate localization.

extensions.text: Lengthen the lateral incision for direct cortical control rather than creating an uncertain percutaneous entry.

indications.text: Use for selected pediatric femoral fractures treated with paired antegrade ESIN, including distal patterns where retrograde entry is unsuitable.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid when proximal anatomy cannot safely accommodate two separated entries or fracture size and stability exceed ESIN capability.

implant_implications.text: Use two appropriately contoured nails with separated entries and balanced opposing forces; avoid prominent ends that irritate lateral tissues.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm physis, entry separation, cortical integrity, canal trajectory, reduction, and nail-end position on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Confirm hemostasis and nonprominent nail ends, repair fascia as needed, then close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include cortical split, physeal injury, malalignment, nail migration or irritation, infection, loss of fixation, and growth disturbance.

bailouts.text: If entry placement or cortex is unsafe, stop, enlarge exposure, revise entry strategy, or choose another fixation construct.

procedure_applications.condition: A pediatric distal-femur or shaft pattern is selected for two-nail antegrade elastic stable intramedullary fixation

questions.question: Where are the usual entries?
questions.answer: On the lateral proximal femur, 0.5-1 cm distal to the greater-trochanteric physis.

questions.question: How far apart should they be?
questions.answer: At least 2 cm axially and 1 cm on the lateral plane.

questions.question: Why avoid closely spaced entries?
questions.answer: They can split the cortex during nail insertion.
